items.title: Live Updates: Exit Polls Suggest No Clear Winner in Pivotal Israeli Election
items.summary: A bloc of parties led by the former military chief Gadi Eisenkot is trying to unseat Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu and his right-wing allies. Vote counting continues after a day of strong voter turnout.
items.full_text: Israelis voted in the largest numbers in a generation on Tuesday, and exit polls suggested that a bloc of opposition parties was roughly even with Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu’s alliance in what many described as a make-or-break moment for the nation. The election did not appear to immediately determine who would lead the country next. Vote counting was expected to last days, followed by a potentially lengthy effort by the blocs to assemble a parliamentary majority. The exit polls, if accurate, pointed to at least one surprise in projecting that two Arab parties would win as many as 17 or 18 seats in the 120-seat Parliament, which would be their strongest showing ever. Voter turnout in Arab Israeli communities was especially high. The exit polls suggest that neither Mr. Netanyahu’s bloc nor the one led by Gadi Eisenkot , a former military chief whose son was killed in the Gaza war, will be able to form a government on its own without relying on the Arab parties. Mr. Netanyahu’s coalition is highly unlikely to include them, and Mr. Eisenkot and his partners have balked at the idea, too. One option analysts are already weighing is whether Mr. Netanyahu, who has led the most far-right government in Israeli history, could join with Mr. Eisenkot to form a unity government. Mr. Netanyahu’s Likud party appears to have taken the largest share of votes among individual parties, even though the two multiparty alliances may have taken similar numbers. Earlier exit polls had indicated a small lead for the opposition bloc, but the polls were revised as the night went on. The creation of a unity government would face major obstacles, given how deeply Mr. Eisenkot’s voters despise Mr. Netanyahu. And the two would have to agree on which of them would run the government. Mr. Netanyahu is unlikely to give up control, while Mr. Eisenkot has called him unfit to lead Israel. The election was Israel’s first since the Hamas-led Oct. 7 attack in 2023, which was the deadliest day for Jews since the Holocaust and ignited three years of war that left Gaza largely in ruins and nearly all its population displaced. Much remained unclear as of Tuesday evening. Making matters even murkier, Israel’s exit polls have a spotty history of accuracy, particularly in tight races. Mr. Netanyahu was expected to address his supporters soon. Mr. Eisenkot appeared onstage past midnight at his post-election party and attempted to strike a tone of triumph — as well as defiance toward Mr. Netanyahu. “Tonight we got the answer: The public wants change,” he said, before making a pointed reference to his main opponent. Amid reports that Mr. Netanyahu has been pushing for renewed attacks on Iran, Eisenkot warned him not to abuse his power as prime minister to influence the process of forming a new government. “Netanyahu, don’t dare use Israel’s security for your political needs,” he said. In the coming days, after official vote totals are released and parliamentary seats are allocated to parties, Israel’s president, Isaac Herzog, will invite the party leader he thinks has the best chance to assemble a governing coalition. Such a coalition would usually have to be made up of at least 61 lawmakers. One factor not reflected in exit polls are the hundreds of thousands of votes cast by Israelis at special polling stations, including at military bases, hospitals, prisons and embassies. In the previous election, those votes tended to favor the coalition of Mr. Netanyahu and his allies. Responding to the high turnout in largely Arab towns, Mr. Netanyahu accused Arab citizens of “trying to steal the elections,” repeatedly making overt appeals to anti-Arab prejudice to push his right-wing base to vote. Dean Livne, the acting director of the Central Election Committee, told reporters that there were no reports of widespread irregularities. Yousef Jabareen, who leads an alliance of Arab parties, said the prime minister was “inciting against Arab citizens and undermining the legitimacy of our vote.” “I’m telling you: The Arab community knows how to punish you,” Mr. Jabareen said on social media. “Today we’re sending you and your bloodstained government packing.” Mr. Netanyahu’s bloc offered the promise of a more religious Israel with an ever-tighter grip over the Israeli-occupied West Bank and Gaza. Mr. Eisenkot’s bloc portrayed the vote as the last chance to preserve liberal democracy and pull Israel back from the brink of becoming a pariah state under international sanctions. Leaders of Mr. Eisenkot’s alliance also called for a reckoning over what they call Mr. Netanyahu’s failure to prevent the Oct. 7 attacks, and pledged to repair Israel’s shattered image abroad , including by cracking down on Israeli extremist violence against Palestinians in the occupied West Bank. Mr. Netanyahu has resisted the establishment of an independent commission to investigate the Oct. 7 attacks. He has vowed to move ahead with overhauling Israel’s judicial system, which critics say could undermine the country’s democracy. And his allies say they hope to permanently entrench Israeli rule in the West Bank and Gaza. Mansour Abbas, the leader of Raam, told a television interviewer that the turnout showed that Arab voters, who make up about 20 percent of Israel’s population, had channeled their “frustration and despair” into “hope.” He said he wanted to replace Mr. Netanyahu’s government “in every possible way” and that his first priority was to “ensure that there is a chance of forming a government” that achieved that goal. The Arab parties’ strong showing may make them kingmakers. But building a governing coalition with Arab participation remains a fraught exercise in Israel. Many Israeli Jews believe that a parliamentary majority should not rely on the support of Arab lawmakers. People waiting to cast ballots in Umm al-Fahm, one of the largest Arab towns in Israel, on Tuesday. Credit... Ahmad Gharabli/Agence France-Presse — Getty Images Arab citizens make up about 20 percent of Israel’s population, and most are the descendants of Palestinians who remained in their homes during the 1948 Arab-Israel war at the time of Israel’s independence. Today, they mostly live in separate towns from Jewish Israelis and face violence and discriminatory housing policies. Over the decades, disagreements, including over Israel’s nature as a Jewish state, have led many Arab voters to avoid the ballot box. This week, many Arab voters said they were furious at Mr. Netanyahu for his treatment of the Palestinians in the West Bank and Gaza and for policies that they feel treat Palestinians in Israel as second-class citizens. Indeed, throughout the campaign, Mr. Netanyahu made overt appeals to anti-Arab prejudice. Of the two Arab parties that did well on Tuesday, only Raam has joined a coalition government in the past. That happened in 2021, when it joined the short-lived anti-Netanyahu coalition of Prime Minister Naftali Bennett. Raam’s participation in that government outraged many right-wing Jewish voters, and when it collapsed after roughly one year, they backed Mr. Netanyahu, who went on to form the most hard-line government in Israel’s history. That government now faces the possibility that it may be brought down by an election result that has been deeply shaped by robust Arab turnout. The longevity of his most recent governing coalition followed three years during which a cycle of collapsed coalitions and five snap elections had left the country without a functional government or national budget. In 2021, Israelis ousted Mr. Netanyahu from power and then returned him to office 18 months later. He had staged a previous comeback, in 2009, becoming prime minister a decade after his party was voted out of power. March 2021 Ousted by a single-seat majority In 2021, Mr. Netanyahu’s government collapsed after failing to pass a budget, setting off legislative elections. At the time, he had been indicted on charges of fraud, bribery and breach of trust , and the coalition he was leading was shaky. According to analysts , heading into an election was a gambit by Mr. Netanyahu to strengthen his grip on power before his criminal trial. But the electorate that voted that March didn’t give him the seats he needed, ending a period of 12 straight years in office for him. It took months of wrangling for an eclectic coalition of anti-Netanyahu forces to cobble together a single-seat majority in the Parliament. Naftali Bennett, a right-wing former ally of Mr. Netanyahu’s, led the coalition as prime minister, hammering out a deal with Yair Lapid, a centrist and former broadcaster who was appointed foreign minister. The eight-party coalition proved too unwieldy to endure. After two right-wing lawmakers defected and several on the left rebelled in critical votes, that government collapsed in June 2022 . November 2022 Returned to office by a hard-line coalition After the resulting elections, held in November 2022, Mr. Netanyahu returned to power as right-wing voters moved to more extreme parties, diminishing the center left. Mr. Netanyahu’s Likud party allied with far-right and ultra-Orthodox lawmakers to secure a clear majority in the Parliament , forming the most hard-line and religious conservative government in Israel’s history. The coalition accounted for 48.4 percent of the vote but had a parliamentary majority because two anti-Netanyahu parties — one leftist, one Arab nationalist — fell just short of the share of votes needed to obtain seats. It was a reminder of how tiny swings among voters can have a big effect under Israel’s parliamentary system. Mr. Netanyahu has since overseen an acceleration of the country’s rightward shift, including an effort to overhaul the judiciary that prompted huge street protests. Questions about whether his government could have better pre-empted the Oct. 7 attack have also become hot-button issues .
